title: SupplementManifest
description: What supplementary material exists for ONE paper, where it is on disk, and what each part of it contains. A fetch cache plus a content index: the fetch half records how each file arrived (including by hand), the index half names the tables worth reading and their columns, so a later reader can go straight to a sheet instead of re-scanning heterogeneous files. Not curated config — never merge this into cas.json.

manifest_version.description: Bumped when the manifest shape changes in a way that invalidates existing stores.

indexed_at.description: ISO-8601 UTC timestamp of the last time the content index below was (re)written.

files.description: Every supplementary file known for this paper, whether or not it was retrieved. One entry per file as the publisher packages it; members of an archive are listed in `members`, not here.

tables.description: The content index: tables worth reading, wherever they live (a sheet in a workbook, a CSV inside a zip, a table in a document). This is what downstream steps consult to decide what to open.

prose.description: The content index for supplementary material that is prose rather than a table: a Supplementary Discussion, a Methods section, a table-legends document. It has no header row and no columns, so `tables` cannot hold it, and a bundle whose legends document is unrepresentable reads as though it were absent. Prose is not sliced by a query the way a table is — it is read whole into a reader's context — so each pointer carries the path to its extracted text, and `sections` carries the spans of it worth reading.

gaps.description: Things the indexer could not do, stated explicitly so an absence is never mistaken for a negative result. Read this before concluding a paper has no marker tables.

Paper.description: Which paper this manifest belongs to. `doi` is the store key. Deliberately minimal: role, title, organism and the rest belong to the CAS+ document that defines the corpus, and duplicating them into a fetch cache only creates something that can drift out of date.

pmcid.description: Cached because the fetch routes are keyed on it and resolving DOI -> PMCID costs a network call. A fetch detail, not curated metadata.

SupplementFile.description: One supplementary file as the publisher packages it, plus how (or whether) we got hold of it.

file_id.description: Stable id for cross-referencing from TablePointer. The publisher's filename, e.g. '41586_2024_8002_MOESM4_ESM.zip'.

label.description: The publisher's label, verbatim, e.g. 'Supplementary Tables'. From JATS <supplementary-material><label>.

caption.description: The publisher's caption, verbatim, e.g. 'Supplementary Tables 1-40.'. From JATS <caption>. Often the cheapest description of the contents there is — read this before opening anything.

media_type.description: Extension-derived kind: xlsx, csv, tsv, docx, pdf, zip, txt, video, image, other.

path.description: Path to the file on disk, relative to the store root. Absent when status is not 'present'.

status.description: 'present' = on disk. 'listed' = we know it exists but have not fetched it. 'skipped' = deliberately not fetched (see retrieval.note — usually a size cap or a video). 'unavailable' = no route exists (closed access, needs a manual drop). 'failed' = a route was tried and errored.

members.description: For archives: the unpacked member tree. Paths are relative to the archive root and are what TablePointer.member_path refers to.

relevance.description: Whether this file bears on describing cell types, their properties, or the data supporting them — the only reason this store exists. 'irrelevant' is a positive finding, not a failure to look: it is what stops a 13 MB peer-review PDF being re-examined on every pass and explains why a stored file has no table pointers. 'unknown' means the cheap signals did not settle it and a reader should.

relevance_note.description: What the verdict was based on, e.g. 'caption: Peer Review file', 'columns: names/logfoldchanges/pvals_adj -> DEG results'. Keeps the judgement auditable and re-runnable.

Retrieval.description: How this file arrived. A file dropped in by hand is a first-class route, not a failure — it is the only route for closed-access papers.

route.description: 'jats_listing' = known from the article XML but bytes not fetched by this route. 'publisher_direct' = fetched from the publisher's static host. 'europepmc_bundle' = from Europe PMC's supplementaryFiles zip. 'biorxiv' = listed on, and fetched from, the preprint's bioRxiv page. 'manual' = supplied by a user. 'none' = no route available.

attempted_at.description: When a route was last tried and did NOT produce bytes. This is the negative cache: a file that is 'unavailable' or 'failed' with this set is not retried on a later run unless a retry is asked for, which is what stops a missing supplement being re-requested on every pass.

sha256.description: Digest of the file as stored, so a re-index can tell whether the bytes changed.

note.description: Why a route was skipped or how it failed. Free text.

path.description: Where the member was unpacked to, relative to the store root. Absent if it was not unpacked.

relevance.description: Whether this file bears on describing cell types, their properties, or the data supporting them — the only reason this store exists. 'irrelevant' is a positive finding, not a failure to look: it is what stops a 13 MB peer-review PDF being re-examined on every pass and explains why a stored file has no table pointers. 'unknown' means the cheap signals did not settle it and a reader should.

relevance_note.description: What the verdict was based on, e.g. 'caption: Peer Review file', 'columns: names/logfoldchanges/pvals_adj -> DEG results'. Keeps the judgement auditable and re-runnable.

TablePointer.description: A table worth reading, located precisely enough to slice without searching, and carrying its own relevance verdict. One pointer per table — a sheet, not a workbook — because a 42-sheet supplement routinely mixes differential expression with antibody lists, and a verdict on the file as a whole cannot express that. Describes the table and its columns; it records WHETHER cell types are named but deliberately does NOT enumerate WHICH (a query-time question). A table is never read into a reader's context wholesale — that is what the locator and columns are for.

file_id.description: The SupplementFile.file_id this table lives in.

member_path.description: Path within the archive, when file_id names an archive.

locator.description: Where in the file: a worksheet name for xlsx, a page number for pdf, a heading for docx. Omit for a single-table file such as a CSV.

table_label.description: The authors' own name for it, verbatim where one exists, e.g. 'Supplementary Table 12'.

content_type.description: What kind of table this is. 'deg_results' differential expression; 'marker_list' asserted markers; 'cluster_annotation' a cluster-to-name mapping; 'cell_metadata' one row per cell; 'sample_metadata' one row per sample or donor; 'enrichment' GSEA/GO results; 'interaction' ligand-receptor or cell-cell interactions; 'gene_set' the gene lists an analysis consumed (an input, not a finding); 'reagents' antibodies, primers and probes; 'legend' the contents or data-dictionary sheet that describes the others — worth reading first. 'other' is a real answer, not a default: use it when the table is none of these.

relevance.description: Whether THIS TABLE bears on describing cell types, their properties or the data supporting them. Recorded per table because relevance varies within a file: the same workbook holds the DEG table a report needs and the antibody list it never will. 'irrelevant' is a positive finding — the pointer still exists so the table is accounted for rather than silently absent.

relevance_note.description: What the verdict was based on, e.g. 'caption: Peer Review file', 'columns: names/logfoldchanges/pvals_adj -> DEG results'. Keeps the judgement auditable and re-runnable.

description.description: What the table contains and what a reader would use it for. One or two sentences, grounded in the caption, the legend sheet, or the headers actually seen.

columns.description: The table's columns in order, each with what it holds. The point of the manifest: a reader picks a table by its columns without opening it. For a very wide table (one column per cell state, say) this may be a prefix — compare its length against n_columns.

n_columns.description: Total columns in the table. Greater than the length of `columns` when that list is a prefix of a very wide table.

header_row.description: 0-based index of the header row, so a reader can slice correctly. Publisher tables often carry title rows above the header.

n_rows.description: Data rows excluding the header, where known.

evidence.description: What this characterisation was based on: 'caption', 'legend_sheet', 'headers', or 'rows_read'. Distinguishes a table described from its caption from one actually opened.

description.description: What the column holds, where the header alone is not self-explanatory.

ProsePointer.description: A piece of supplementary prose and what it contains. Unlike a table, prose is not sliced by a query — the spans that fold in are read whole alongside the paper text, so the pointer carries the path to its extracted text plus the spans worth reading, rather than a locator into the original file. Extraction is recorded because it is not all equal: text recovered from a PDF has no reliable reading order across columns and is not equivalent to JATS when grounding a quote.

file_id.description: The SupplementFile.file_id this prose came from.

member_path.description: Path within the archive, when file_id names an archive.

text_file.description: Store-relative path to the extracted plain text. What a reader opens; the original file may be a format it cannot read.

n_chars.description: Characters of extracted text. The size of the read a caller is committing to.

extractor.description: What produced the text, so its trustworthiness is visible without opening it. 'docx' and 'plaintext' preserve reading order; 'pdf' does not, and text from it must not be treated as equivalent to JATS when grounding a quote.

description.description: What this prose contains and what a reader would use it for. One or two sentences, grounded in the text actually read.

folds_in.description: Whether any of this prose bears on the six report dimensions in `ProseSection.dimensions` — names or synonyms, hierarchy, location, markers, structure, function. This is the fold-in decision for the document as a whole, and for a unit with no sections it is the only one there is. It replaces an earlier `mentions_cell_types`, which asked whether the prose named cell types at all: on an atlas corpus that is true of essentially every supplement, so it excluded nothing and the fold-in it gated was the entire bundle. Where `sections` carry their own `folds_in`, this is true if any of them is.

folds_in_note.description: What the verdict rests on, and whether the view behind it was the document or part of it. A `false` from an `outline` or `sampled_text` view covers what was seen, never the document, and nothing downstream may upgrade it.

sections.description: The document's sections, in order, with where each one sits in `text_file`. Present when the format records its own structure — Word paragraph styles, or the markdown headings pymupdf4llm reports for a PDF. This is what keeps a long document usable: a 53,000-character supplement whose `Cell type annotation` section is 2,773 characters can contribute those, not all of it, and a legends document can be read one figure at a time while its references section — routinely two thirds of the file — is left alone.

evidence.description: What the description was based on. 'full_text' is the document itself — short enough to read, so the verdict is about all of it. 'outline' is its section headings only, available where the extractor reports them; 'sampled_text' is head, middle and tail. Under either of the latter two a negative verdict covers what was seen, not the document.

ProseSection.description: One run of a document under a single heading, and where to find it. Offsets index `text_file` directly, so a reader slices the extracted text without re-parsing the original — which for a PDF would mean re-running the extractor, and for a docx re-reading the archive.

heading.description: The heading, verbatim, truncated to 80 characters. For a legends document this is the figure or table it describes.

char_start.description: 0-based character offset of the section's first paragraph in `text_file`.

char_end.description: Character offset one past the section's last paragraph, so `text[char_start:char_end]` is exactly the section.

folds_in.description: Whether this span is read into a reader's context. Set when the document was judged section-wise, which is the only thing that makes a long supplement affordable: across the reproductive corpus this decision removes about 42% of long-form prose, and on a methods-dominated document up to 92%. ABSENT IS NOT FALSE. The outline handed to a judge omits the smallest sections, so a span with no `folds_in` was never shown to anyone and is unjudged — fold it in, or judge it, but do not read the silence as a decision. A `false` means a judge saw the heading and ruled it out.

dimensions.description: Which of the six report dimensions this span plausibly bears on, and so why it folds in. Recorded because a reader chasing markers and one chasing location want different spans of the same document. Judged from a heading, so it is a claim about what the span is likely to cover, not a promise that it does. Empty or absent alongside `folds_in: false` means none of the six.

items.description: 'names' — what a population is called, its synonyms, or a cluster-ID-to-name mapping. 'hierarchy' — broad lineage against fine subtype, or parent/child relations between populations. 'location' — tissue, compartment, spatial or developmental-stage context. 'markers' — genes or proteins that identify a population. 'structure' — its morphology. 'function' — what it does.

CasUptake.description: A note that content from this unit was taken into the project's CAS+ document at setup. Written by whatever performed the uptake, because only it knows what it took. It exists so a later run can tell a CAS-supplied fact from a paper-found one, and so a re-run does not re-derive what is already curated.

at.description: ISO-8601 UTC timestamp of the uptake.

note.description: What was taken and into which part of CAS+, in a sentence.

Gap.description: Something the indexer could not do. Keeps 'we did not look' distinguishable from 'there is nothing there'.

reason.description: Why it could not be characterised, e.g. 'archive member exceeds size cap', 'scanned PDF, no extractable text', 'no route to fetch (closed access)'.

action.description: What a human could do about it, e.g. 'drop the file into incoming/'. Omit if nothing would help.
